verifiedClaims.claim: claim denials are far more common than most people expect
verifiedClaims.note: Frequency claim with no primary source. No regulator publishes a denial rate for bodily-injury liability claims in either state. Delete the clause or reword to something the post can stand behind ('a denial is common enough that both states regulate how insurers handle claims').

verifiedClaims.claim: Insurance companies in both Georgia and South Carolina deny legitimate personal injury claims every day, often counting on injured claimants to give up rather than fight back.
verifiedClaims.note: Unsourced population claim about insurer motive and frequency. If a replacement is wanted, the statutes name the conduct: South Carolina lists 'Compelling policyholders or claimants, including third-party claimants under liability policies, to institute suits ... by offering substantially less than the amounts ultimately recovered' as an improper claim practice (S.C. Code § 38-59-20(5)); Georgia lists the same conduct for 'insureds or beneficiaries' (O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34(5)).

verifiedClaims.claim: According to the Cornell Law Institute's overview of insurance bad faith, policyholders and third-party claimants have legal remedies when insurers fail to handle claims in good faith.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The linked page is the Wex entry 'bad faith' from the Legal Information Institute (LII) at Cornell Law School. Its entire text is a one-paragraph definition ('Bad faith refers to dishonesty or fraud in a transaction ... often related to a breach of the obligation inherent in all contracts to deal with the other parties in good faith and with fair dealing'), last reviewed June 2022. It says nothing about insurance, policyholders, third-party claimants or remedies.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute — Wex: bad faith
verifiedClaims.note: Two errors. (1) The sentence attributes to Cornell a proposition Cornell does not make, and the organisation is the 'Legal Information Institute at Cornell Law School', not the 'Cornell Law Institute'. (2) The proposition itself is wrong in both states for third-party claimants: Georgia's § 33-4-6 runs only to the policyholder and § 33-4-7 is limited to property damage (Mills v. Allstate, 288 Ga. App. 257 (2007)); South Carolina 'does not recognize a third party action for the bad faith refusal to pay insurance benefits' (Kleckley v. Northwestern Nat'l Cas. Co., 338 S.C. 131 (2000)). Keep the link only as a definition of the term: 'Bad faith, in the Legal Information Institute's definition, is dishonesty in a transaction — here, an insurer refusing to deal fairly with a claim.'

verifiedClaims.claim: In states like Georgia, where the modified comparative fault threshold under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33 bars recovery at 50% or more fault, adjusters will aggressively push the narrative that you caused the accident.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(g): 'the plaintiff shall not be entitled to receive any damages if the plaintiff is 50 percent or more responsible for the injury or damages claimed.'
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33 (verified verbatim in sibling packs 1709, 1722, 1724 on 2026-09-23/24)
verifiedClaims.note: Matches the writer-profile table. 'Adjusters will aggressively push' is opinion, not a fact claim.

verifiedClaims.claim: One of the most overused denial tactics.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: A common denial ground.
verifiedClaims.note: Superlative with no ranking source. The rest of the 'common reasons' list (disputed liability, lapsed or insufficient coverage, pre-existing conditions, gaps in treatment, missed deadlines, recorded statements) is stated as practice, not law, and can stay.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia and South Carolina both follow the "eggshell plaintiff" doctrine, meaning a defendant takes the victim as they find them — but that does not stop insurers from trying.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina: 'a defendant takes the plaintiff as he or she is found, and the plaintiff is entitled to recover damages resulting from the aggravation of a pre-existing condition' (Burnett v. Family Kingdom, Inc., 387 S.C. 183, 691 S.E.2d 170 (Ct. App. 2010), citing Waring v. Johnson, 341 S.C. 248, 260 (Ct. App. 2000)). Georgia: the 'eggshell plaintiff' charge is a recognised jury instruction — the Court of Appeals reviewed a judgment in which the trial court 'instruct[ed] the jury on concurrent negligence and the "eggshell" plaintiff' (Tucker Nursing Center, Inc. v. Mosby, 303 Ga. App. 80, 692 S.E.2d 727 (2010)), and a 2025 appeal (Thomas v. Accurate Steel Rule Cutting Die, A25A0073) turned on a refusal to give that instruction.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Burnett v. Family Kingdom, Inc. (S.C. Ct. App. 2010); Tucker Nursing Center, Inc. v. Mosby (Ga. Ct. App. 2010)
verifiedClaims.note: Optional citations in the sentence: '(Burnett v. Family Kingdom, S.C. Ct. App. 2010)' for South Carolina. Georgia support is the instruction's existence rather than a quotable rule statement; if a Georgia citation is added, Tucker Nursing is the verified one (https://law.justia.com/cases/georgia/court-of-appeals/2010/a09a1756.html).

verifiedClaims.claim: Insurance companies in Georgia and South Carolina are required to provide a written explanation when they deny a claim.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: it is an unfair claims settlement practice, 'When requested by the insured in writing, failing in the case of claims denial or offers of compromise settlement to provide promptly a reasonable and accurate explanation of the basis for such actions. In the case of claims denials, such denials shall be in writing' (O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34(10)) — a duty owed to the insured, on written request, and enforced by the Commissioner. South Carolina's improper-claim-practices list (S.C. Code § 38-59-20) has no written-denial item; the closest duties are acknowledging communications with reasonable promptness (2) and not misrepresenting pertinent facts or policy provisions to insureds or third-party claimants (1).
verifiedClaims.note: Overstated as written. Suggested: 'In Georgia an insurer must put a denial in writing and, if its policyholder asks in writing, explain the basis for it (O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34(10)). No statute gives a claimant against another driver's insurer the same right in either state — so ask for the reasons in writing regardless; a refusal to explain is itself worth documenting.' The next sentence ('If you received a verbal denial ... send a written request') already gives the right practical advice.

verifiedClaims.claim: Deadlines for filing an appeal or providing additional information
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Any deadline the letter sets for a response or for additional information
verifiedClaims.note: Denial-letter checklist bullet. There is no statutory appeal from a liability insurer's denial in either state (see the Step 3 entry); 'appeal' should not appear as if it were a procedure with a deadline.

verifiedClaims.claim: Most insurance policies include an internal appeals process. Filing a formal appeal forces the insurer to re-examine your claim, often with a different adjuster or supervisor reviewing the file.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: There is no statutory or contractual 'appeal' of a liability insurer's denial of a third-party bodily-injury claim in Georgia or South Carolina: the claimant is not a party to the policy, and nothing 'forces' the insurer to re-examine the claim except its regulatory duties (a reasonable investigation before refusing to pay, O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34(6); reasonable standards for prompt investigation and settlement of third-party liability claims, S.C. Code § 38-59-20(3)) and, ultimately, a lawsuit. Asking in writing for reconsideration with new evidence is sound practice, but it is a request, not a procedure. Where the denial comes from the reader's own insurer (UM/UIM, med-pay, PIP), the policy's dispute provisions and a complaint to the regulator apply.
verifiedClaims.note: Most consequential structural error after the bad-faith misattribution. 'Most insurance policies include an internal appeals process' is unverifiable and, for auto liability policies, not how they work (formal internal appeals with deadlines are a health-plan feature). Rename Step 3 'Ask for Reconsideration in Writing', and rewrite the paragraph so the reader knows the letter carries no legal force of its own — its force is the evidence it carries and the lawsuit it precedes. The bullet list under it ('A strong appeal letter should ...') is fine as a reconsideration-letter checklist.

verifiedClaims.claim: Set a reasonable deadline for the insurer to respond (typically 30 days)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Set a deadline for the insurer to respond — in Georgia motor-vehicle cases an attorney-prepared pre-suit offer must give the insurer at least 30 days to accept (O.C.G.A. § 9-11-67.1); South Carolina sets no fixed period.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 9-11-67.1 (verified verbatim in sibling packs 1722 and 1744)
verifiedClaims.note: 'Typically 30 days' has no source; tying the figure to the Georgia statutory floor makes it defensible. Same finding as pack 1722.

verifiedClaims.claim: Insurers know that represented claimants are far more likely to follow through with litigation if the appeal is denied.
verifiedClaims.note: Behavioural claim about insurers and claimants with no primary source (the usual citation is an Insurance Research Council study that is not a primary source and was not verified). Cut the sentence; the preceding sentence about an attorney reviewing the letter stands on its own.

verifiedClaims.claim: Both Georgia and South Carolina have laws prohibiting insurers from handling claims in bad faith, and both states have regulatory agencies that accept consumer complaints.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: Unfair Claims Settlement Practices, O.C.G.A. § 33-6-30 to § 33-6-37 (§ 33-6-34 lists the practices; enforced by the Commissioner, no private action). South Carolina: Improper claim practices, S.C. Code § 38-59-20, which expressly covers 'third-party liability claims' and is enforced by the Director of Insurance under § 38-59-30 (cease-and-desist order and a penalty under § 38-2-10 after notice and hearing, where the practice is 'performed with such frequency as to indicate a general business practice').
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate as a description of the regulatory regimes. Optional: cite the two statutes in the sentence, and say 'claims-handling laws' rather than 'bad faith' laws so the reader does not read a private remedy into them.

verifiedClaims.claim: In Georgia, you can file a complaint with the Georgia Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner. In South Carolina, complaints go to the South Carolina Department of Insurance.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: the Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire (OCI); complaints go to its Consumer Services Division, fastest through the online Consumer Complaint Portal, and OCI asks that you first put the dispute to the insurer and keep records. South Carolina: the Department of Insurance's complaint page (doi.sc.gov/complaint) routes to the NAIC online complaint form for South Carolina (verified 2026-09-23 in pack 1744; doi.sc.gov refused connections from this network on 2026-09-25).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire — File a Consumer Insurance Complaint; South Carolina Department of Insurance — File a Complaint
verifiedClaims.note: Agency name is wrong in the body and the table: the office's own pages and footer read 'Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire'. Link both agencies.

verifiedClaims.claim: These agencies can investigate the insurer's conduct, impose fines, and in some cases compel the insurer to re-open and properly evaluate the claim.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: OCI's stated process: it sends the complaint to the company and 'request[s] a detailed written response', determines whether the issue 'was handled appropriately under the terms of the policy', reviews whether state insurance laws were violated, and will 'Take enforcement action when laws are violated'; if the insurer 'has not investigated the complaint thoroughly, we will require them to do so'; if a law was violated 'we will request corrective action by the company'. South Carolina: after notice and hearing the Director may order the insurer to cease and desist and impose a penalty under § 38-2-10 (§ 38-59-30). Neither agency values the claim or orders the insurer to pay it.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: OCI — File a Consumer Insurance Complaint; S.C. Code § 38-59-30
verifiedClaims.note: 'Compel the insurer to re-open' overstates. Suggested: 'These agencies require the insurer to answer the complaint in writing, can make it investigate thoroughly, and can take enforcement action — fines and cease-and-desist orders — when claims-handling laws are broken. They do not decide what your claim is worth or order the insurer to pay it.' OCI's page also notes its Consumer Services Division has no jurisdiction over self-insured employer plans, federal programs or policies bought in another state.

verifiedClaims.claim: Filing a regulatory complaint also creates an official record of the insurer's conduct. If the case later goes to trial, evidence that you reported the insurer's behavior to state regulators can support a bad faith claim and demonstrate a pattern of unreasonable denial practices.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The 'pattern' matters to the regulator, not to the claimant's trial: South Carolina's statute reaches conduct 'performed with such frequency as to indicate a general business practice' (§ 38-59-20), and Georgia's § 33-6-34 applies 'when committed as provided in Code Section 33-6-33'. A claimant against the at-fault driver's insurer has no bad-faith claim to support (Mills v. Allstate; Kleckley).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 38-59-20; Kleckley v. Northwestern Nat'l Cas. Co., 338 S.C. 131 (2000); Mills v. Allstate Ins. Co., 288 Ga. App. 257 (2007)
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'A regulatory complaint also puts the insurer's conduct on record. Regulators act on patterns — South Carolina's statute reaches practices carried out often enough to be a general business practice — so a complaint that joins others can bring enforcement your own case never would. It does not create a bad-faith claim for you against the other driver's insurer.'

verifiedClaims.claim: In both Georgia and South Carolina, you have the right to pursue a civil claim against the at-fault party — and in some cases, directly against the insurer for bad faith conduct.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The civil claim is against the at-fault party. A direct bad-faith action against the at-fault party's liability insurer is not available to the injured person in either state: Georgia's § 33-4-6 is 'in favor of the insurer's policy holder' and § 33-4-7 is limited to property damage (Mills v. Allstate, 288 Ga. App. 257 (2007)); South Carolina 'does not recognize a third party action for the bad faith refusal to pay insurance benefits' (Kleckley, 338 S.C. 131 (2000)). Bad-faith remedies exist against the reader's own insurer — in Georgia the § 33-4-6 penalty (up to the greater of 50% or $5,000 plus fees, 60-day demand) and, on UM claims, § 33-7-11(j) (up to the greater of 25% or $25,000 plus fees, 60-day demand); in South Carolina attorney's fees after a 90-day demand (§ 38-59-40) and the Nichols tort. The failure-to-settle claim against the at-fault driver's insurer belongs to that driver (Southern General v. Holt, 262 Ga. 267 (1992); Tyger River Pine Co. v. Maryland Cas. Co., 170 S.C. 286 (1933)) and reaches the injured person only by assignment, as in Holt.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Mills v. Allstate Ins. Co. (Ga. Ct. App. 2007); Kleckley v. Northwestern Nat'l Cas. Co. (S.C. 2000); O.C.G.A. §§ 33-4-6, 33-7-11(j); S.C. Code § 38-59-40; Nichols v. State Farm (S.C. 1983); Southern General v. Holt (Ga. 1992) — all verified in sibling packs 1722/1724/1709/1744
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: '... a civil claim against the at-fault party. If the denial came from your own insurer — an uninsured or underinsured motorist claim, for example — you may also have a bad-faith claim against it. You cannot sue the other driver's insurer for bad faith in either state; when that insurer wrongly refuses to settle within its limits, the claim it creates belongs to its own policyholder, who can assign it to you.'

verifiedClaims.claim: In fact, the vast majority of personal injury cases settle after a lawsuit is filed but before trial begins.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Bench and jury trials 'accounted for an estimated 4% of all tort dispositions in 2005' in a national sample of state-court jurisdictions (Bureau of Justice Statistics, Tort Bench and Jury Trials in State Courts, 2005, NCJ 228129, published November 2009). The other 96% ended by settlement, dismissal or other disposition — the report does not separate settlements from dismissals.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Bureau of Justice Statistics — Tort Bench and Jury Trials in State Courts, 2005
verifiedClaims.note: Supports 'the vast majority resolve without a trial', not 'settle'. Suggested: 'In fact, only about 4 percent of tort cases in state courts end in a trial (Bureau of Justice Statistics); the rest are resolved — most of them by settlement — before a jury is seated.' The figure is old (2005 data); there is no newer BJS tort-trial series.

verifiedClaims.claim: Once a lawsuit is filed, the discovery process gives your attorney the ability to subpoena the insurer's claim file, depose the adjusters who handled your case, and obtain internal communications that may reveal whether the denial was made in bad faith.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: In a negligence suit the defendant is the at-fault party, not its insurer; discovery goes to liability and damages (the defendant, witnesses, records, experts). The insurer's claim file, adjuster depositions and internal communications are the subject of a bad-faith action, which in a third-party case belongs to the insured (Holt; Tyger River) — not to the injured claimant.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Southern General Ins. Co. v. Holt, 262 Ga. 267 (1992); Kleckley v. Northwestern Nat'l Cas. Co., 338 S.C. 131 (2000)
verifiedClaims.note: Overpromises what a claimant's suit against the driver yields. Suggested: 'Once a lawsuit is filed, discovery lets your attorney depose the at-fault party and witnesses, subpoena records, and test the facts the insurer relied on. Denials built on a thin file rarely survive that process, which is often what moves the case to settlement.' The specific scope of claim-file discovery was not researched this run; do not assert it either way.

verifiedClaims.claim: Lawsuits are especially common in medical malpractice cases and premises liability claims, where insurers routinely dispute the nature and extent of injuries or argue that the property owner had no duty to prevent the hazard.
verifiedClaims.note: Frequency claim ('especially common', 'routinely') with no source. Keep the internal links by rewording to the defensible point: in malpractice and premises cases the disputes are usually about duty and causation, which are decided on evidence a lawsuit can develop.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia takes insurance bad faith seriously. Under O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6, when an insurer refuses to pay a claim in bad faith and the insured is forced to litigate, the court may award penalties of up to 50% of the claim amount plus reasonable attorney's fees. This statute gives Georgia policyholders a powerful weapon against insurers that deny or delay valid claims without justification.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 33-4-6(a): where the insurer refuses to pay a covered loss 'within 60 days after a demand has been made by the holder of the policy' and the refusal is found to be in bad faith, it is liable to 'such holder' for the loss plus 'not more than 50 percent of the liability of the insurer for the loss or $5,000.00, whichever is greater, and all reasonable attorney's fees'. First-party only; the injured claimant against the at-fault driver's insurer has no claim under it (Mills v. Allstate).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6 (verified verbatim in sibling packs 1722, 1724, 1709, 1744); Mills v. Allstate Ins. Co., 288 Ga. App. 257 (2007)
verifiedClaims.note: The words 'the insured' and 'policyholders' are correct, but the section heading ('Bad Faith Denial Laws in Georgia') and the post's frame (a claim against the at-fault party) lead the reader to take it as their remedy. Add the missing '$5,000, whichever is greater' floor and open the section with one sentence saying whose remedy this is: the policyholder's — for a denied claim against your own insurer (UM/UIM, med-pay) — not the injured person's against the other driver's carrier.

verifiedClaims.claim: To trigger bad faith penalties under O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6, the claimant must send a written demand to the insurer at least 60 days before filing suit. The demand must specify the claim amount and give the insurer an opportunity to pay.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The demand must be 'made by the holder of the policy' — 'the claimant' is the wrong party. 60 days is correct. On uninsured-motorist claims the parallel provision is § 33-7-11(j): 60-day demand, penalty up to the greater of 25% or $25,000 plus fees (sibling pack 1724).
verifiedClaims.note: Change 'the claimant' to 'the policyholder'. The 'must specify the claim amount' detail was not independently verified this run; 'a written demand for payment' is the safe phrasing.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia courts have held that bad faith exists when the insurer had no reasonable basis for denying the claim or when the insurer failed to conduct an adequate investigation.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The Georgia standard under § 33-4-6: "'Bad faith' means a frivolous and unfounded refusal to pay the claim" (Taylor v. Government Employees Ins. Co., 350 Ga. App. 734, 830 S.E.2d 235 (2019)). An inadequate investigation is a regulatory unfair claims settlement practice — 'Refusing to pay claims without conducting a reasonable investigation' (§ 33-6-34(6)) — enforced by the Commissioner, not a private bad-faith ground.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Taylor v. Gov't Emps. Ins. Co., 350 Ga. App. 734 (2019); O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'Georgia courts define bad faith as a frivolous and unfounded refusal to pay; an insurer with a reasonable basis for its position does not owe the penalty even if it loses. A denial without a reasonable investigation is separately an unfair claims settlement practice the Commissioner can act on (O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34).' The Taylor opinion is served as a PDF on Justia; the quoted sentence was read from the CourtListener index of the same opinion (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/7479882/taylor-v-govt-emps-ins-co/).

verifiedClaims.claim: The 50% penalty provision is designed to deter insurers from stonewalling legitimate claims, and Georgia judges do enforce it.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The penalty is 'not more than 50 percent of the liability of the insurer for the loss or $5,000.00, whichever is greater' (§ 33-4-6(a)).
verifiedClaims.note: Fix the amount and cut 'Georgia judges do enforce it' (unsourced, and bad faith under the statute is a fact question, not a judicial choice).

verifiedClaims.claim: For workers' compensation claims in Georgia, a separate set of rules applies under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-221, which allows the State Board of Workers' Compensation to impose penalties when insurers unreasonably deny or delay benefits.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 34-9-221 governs payment and denial procedure, and its penalties are for lateness, not for the merits of a denial: the first income-benefit payment is due 'on the twenty-first day after the employer has knowledge of the injury' (b); an employer that controverts must file a notice to controvert with the Board 'on or before the twenty-first day after knowledge of the alleged injury' stating the grounds (d); benefits payable without an award that are not paid when due carry a 15 percent add-on unless a notice to controvert was filed or the Board excuses the delay (e); benefits under an award not paid within 20 days carry 20 percent (f); once benefits have been paid the right to compensation can be controverted only for change in condition or newly discovered evidence unless a notice to controvert is filed within 60 days of the first payment's due date (h); ten days' notice is required before suspending benefits (i); the Board or an ALJ issues the orders enforcing these penalties (j). Unreasonable denial is addressed separately: the ALJ or Board may assess attorney's fees against a party that 'brought, prosecuted, or defended in whole or in part without reasonable grounds' (§ 34-9-108(b)(1)), and the claimant's fee and costs against an employer that fails to comply with § 34-9-221 'without reasonable grounds' (§ 34-9-108(b)(2)). No separate bad-faith action exists: 'Intentional delay of workers' compensation payments did not give rise to an independent cause of action against the employer or its insurer, as the penalties for such a delay were provided by O.C.G.A. § 34-9-221(e)' (Bright v. Nimmo, 253 Ga. 378 (1984), in the Justia annotations).
verifiedClaims.note: Half right. The section is the right citation for the denial procedure and the late-payment penalties; 'unreasonably deny' points to § 34-9-108(b). Suggested: 'Workers' compensation denials follow their own rules. In Georgia the insurer must either start income benefits or file a notice to controvert within 21 days of learning of the injury (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-221); benefits paid late carry a 15 percent penalty (20 percent when an award is unpaid), and the State Board can assess attorney's fees against an insurer that defends a claim without reasonable grounds (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-108). There is no separate bad-faith lawsuit for a delayed comp claim — the Board's penalties are the remedy.' For state parity add South Carolina: a denied claim is decided at a hearing before the Workers' Compensation Commission on the employee's request (S.C. Code § 42-17-20) — Form 50, Employee's Notice of Claim and/or Request for Hearing (a $50 fee applies when a hearing is requested) — and the claim must be filed within two years of the accident (§ 42-15-40). The Board's WC-3 form name is a Board rule, not in the statute; say 'notice to controvert'.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina addresses insurance bad faith through both statutory and common law. S.C. Code § 38-59-20 prohibits unfair claims settlement practices, including failing to acknowledge and act promptly on claims, failing to adopt reasonable standards for investigating claims, and refusing to pay claims without conducting a reasonable investigation.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 38-59-20, 'Improper claim practices', lists eight practices that are improper 'if committed without just cause and performed with such frequency as to indicate a general business practice', including '(2) Failing to acknowledge with reasonable promptness pertinent communications with respect to claims ... including third-party claims arising under liability insurance policies', '(3) Failing to adopt and implement reasonable standards for the prompt investigation and settlement of claims, including third-party liability claims', '(4) Not attempting in good faith to effect prompt, fair, and equitable settlement of claims, including third-party liability claims, submitted to it in which liability has become reasonably clear', and '(8) Any other practice which constitutes an unreasonable delay in paying or an unreasonable failure to pay or settle in full claims, including third-party liability claims'. 'Refusing to pay claims without conducting a reasonable investigation' is Georgia's § 33-6-34(6), not on the South Carolina list. Enforcement is by the Director of Insurance (§ 38-59-30); it creates no private claim, and South Carolina recognises no third-party bad-faith action (Kleckley).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 38-59-20, 38-59-30; Kleckley v. Northwestern Nat'l Cas. Co., 338 S.C. 131 (2000)
verifiedClaims.note: Replace the third example with one that is in the statute (good-faith settlement where liability is reasonably clear, § 38-59-20(4)), say the statute is regulatory and expressly covers third-party liability claims, and note the 'general business practice' threshold.

verifiedClaims.claim: Unlike Georgia's statutory penalty structure, South Carolina allows injured parties to bring a private cause of action for bad faith denial. In the landmark case Nichols v. State Farm, the South Carolina Supreme Court recognized that insureds can sue their own insurer for bad faith refusal to pay benefits. Successful bad faith claims in South Carolina can result in compensatory damages, consequential damages, and in cases of egregious conduct, punitive damages.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The private action belongs to insureds, not 'injured parties': Nichols v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 279 S.C. 336, 306 S.E.2d 616 (1983) recognised a tort action by an insured for bad-faith refusal to pay first-party benefits, with consequential damages beyond the contract and punitive damages for wilful or reckless conduct; Kleckley (2000) holds there is no third-party action. South Carolina also has a statutory remedy the post omits: an insurer that refuses to pay its policyholder's claim for 90 days after demand 'without reasonable cause or in bad faith' owes reasonable attorney's fees, capped at one-third of the judgment (§ 38-59-40(1)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Nichols v. State Farm (S.C. 1983); Kleckley (S.C. 2000); S.C. Code § 38-59-40
verifiedClaims.note: Change 'injured parties' to 'policyholders'; the second and third sentences are accurate for an insured's claim. Add the § 38-59-40 fee remedy so the 'Pre-Suit Demand' table row can be corrected.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina's approach can actually result in larger recoveries than Georgia's 50% penalty in some cases, because punitive damages in bad faith insurance cases are not capped at a fixed percentage of the claim. If the insurer's conduct was particularly outrageous — for example, destroying evidence or deliberately misrepresenting policy terms — a jury can award punitive damages that far exceed the original claim value.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina punitive damages are capped: 'an award of punitive damages may not exceed the greater of three times the amount of compensatory damages awarded to each claimant entitled thereto or the sum of five hundred thousand dollars' (§ 15-32-530(A)); four times or $2,000,000 where the conduct was motivated by unreasonable financial gain with management knowledge or could be a felony (B); no cap for intent to harm, a felony conviction arising from the conduct, or substantial impairment by alcohol or drugs (C). The dollar floor is indexed to CPI each year (D): the Revenue and Fiscal Affairs Office's 2026 memo (February 3, 2026) sets it at $739,245, effective on publication in the State Register.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 15-32-530; S.C. Revenue and Fiscal Affairs Office — 2026 Punitive Damage Award Limitation memo
verifiedClaims.note: Contradicts the post's own table row ('punitive damages capped by S.C. Code § 15-32-530') and the writer profile ('never say SC has no cap'). 'Not capped at a fixed percentage of the claim' is technically true (the cap is a multiple of compensatory damages or a dollar floor) but the paragraph reads as 'uncapped'. Suggested: 'Because the South Carolina remedy is a tort claim, a policyholder's recovery is measured by the harm the denial caused rather than by a percentage of the claim, and punitive damages — capped at the greater of three times compensatory damages or an inflation-adjusted floor (§ 15-32-530; $739,245 for 2026) — are available for wilful or reckless conduct.' RFA memo: https://rfa.sc.gov/sites/rfa/files/2026-03/2026%20Punitive%20Damages%20Awards%20Limitation%20Inflation%20Memo%20signed.pdf (image PDF; read visually).

verifiedClaims.claim: This is an important consideration in pedestrian accident claims and motorcycle accident cases in South Carolina, where insurers sometimes attempt to exploit bias against these claimants to justify unreasonably low offers or outright denials.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The 'consideration' (a bad-faith tort with punitive damages) does not apply to a pedestrian's or motorcyclist's claim against the at-fault driver's insurer (Kleckley); it applies to their claim against their own UM/UIM carrier.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Kleckley v. Northwestern Nat'l Cas. Co., 338 S.C. 131 (2000)
verifiedClaims.note: Keep the internal links but re-point the sentence: pedestrians and motorcyclists are often hit by uninsured or minimally insured drivers, so the claim that gets denied is frequently the UM/UIM claim against their own insurer — and that is the claim the Nichols remedy protects.

verifiedClaims.claim: Bad Faith Statute | O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6 | S.C. Code § 38-59-20
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Row should distinguish the two kinds of law. Bad-faith remedy against your own insurer: Georgia O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6 (UM claims: § 33-7-11(j)); South Carolina S.C. Code § 38-59-40 and the Nichols tort. Claims-handling law enforced by the regulator (no private suit): Georgia O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34; South Carolina S.C. Code § 38-59-20.
verifiedClaims.note: Comparison table. Pairing § 33-4-6 (a private penalty) with § 38-59-20 (a regulatory list) compares unlike things; split into two rows.

verifiedClaims.claim: Bad Faith Penalty | Up to 50% of claim + attorney's fees | Compensatory and consequential damages (uncapped); punitive damages capped by S.C. Code § 15-32-530
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: the greater of 50% of the loss or $5,000, plus attorney's fees (§ 33-4-6) — policyholder only. South Carolina: attorney's fees up to one-third of the judgment after a 90-day demand (§ 38-59-40); under Nichols, consequential damages and, for wilful or reckless conduct, punitive damages capped by § 15-32-530 (greater of 3x compensatory or the indexed floor, $739,245 in 2026) — policyholder only.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6; S.C. Code §§ 38-59-40, 15-32-530; Nichols v. State Farm
verifiedClaims.note: Comparison table. The South Carolina cell's cap statement is right; the Georgia cell omits the $5,000 floor; both need the first-party limit stated in the row label ('against your own insurer').

verifiedClaims.claim: Pre-Suit Demand Required | Yes — 60-day written demand before filing | No statutory pre-suit demand requirement
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: yes — a written demand by the policyholder, 60 days before suit (§ 33-4-6; § 33-7-11(j) for UM). South Carolina: yes for the statutory fee remedy — 90 days after the policyholder's demand (§ 38-59-40); no demand period for the Nichols tort claim.
verifiedClaims.note: Comparison table. Same direct error found in pack 1722 ('There is no 60-day demand window comparable to Georgia's statute'); § 38-59-40 is the South Carolina counterpart.

verifiedClaims.claim: Private Right of Action | Yes, under O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6 | Yes, recognized in Nichols v. State Farm
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: yes for the policyholder (§ 33-4-6); none for an injured third party against the at-fault driver's insurer (Mills v. Allstate; § 33-4-7 covers property damage only). South Carolina: yes for the insured (Nichols); none for a third-party claimant (Kleckley).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Mills v. Allstate Ins. Co., 288 Ga. App. 257 (2007); Kleckley v. Northwestern Nat'l Cas. Co., 338 S.C. 131 (2000)

verifiedClaims.currentValue: O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33: actions for injuries to the person within two years after the right of action accrues. S.C. Code § 15-3-530(5): within three years, 'an action for assault, battery, or any injury to the person or rights of another, not arising on contract'.
verifiedClaims.note: Matches the writer-profile table; § 15-3-530 re-read on scstatehouse.gov this run, § 9-3-33 verified in every sibling pack.

verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: § 51-12-33(g). South Carolina: 'a plaintiff may only recover damages if his or her own negligence is not greater than that of the defendant' (Burnett v. Family Kingdom, 387 S.C. 183 (Ct. App. 2010), restating Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (1991)).

verifiedClaims.claim: Punitive Damages Cap | $250,000 (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1) | Generally 3x compensatory or $500,000 (whichever is greater)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: $250,000 under § 51-12-5.1(g); no cap for product liability (e) or where the defendant acted with specific intent to harm or while impaired by alcohol or drugs (f). South Carolina: greater of 3x compensatory or $500,000 (§ 15-32-530(A)), the dollar figure indexed annually under (D) — $739,245 for 2026 per the Revenue and Fiscal Affairs Office; 4x / $2,000,000 under (B); no cap under (C), including an impaired defendant.

verifiedClaims.note: Comparison table; both cells correct and 'generally' is the right hedge. Optional: add '(S.C. Code § 15-32-530; the $500,000 floor is inflation-adjusted each year — $739,245 for 2026)' and a shared footnote that neither state caps punitive damages against a drunk or drugged driver.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia: 2 years. Under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33, you have two years from the date of injury to file a personal injury lawsuit in Georgia. This is one of the shorter deadlines in the Southeast, and it can sneak up on claimants who are focused on the insurance process rather than the litigation timeline.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Two years under § 9-3-33 is correct. The regional comparison ('one of the shorter deadlines in the Southeast') would require verifying every neighbouring state's limitation period and was not done this run.
verifiedClaims.note: Delete 'This is one of the shorter deadlines in the Southeast, and'; keep 'It can sneak up on claimants ...'.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina: 3 years. Under S.C. Code § 15-3-530, South Carolina allows three years from the date of injury to file suit.
verifiedClaims.note: Verified verbatim on scstatehouse.gov 2026-09-25.

verifiedClaims.claim: There are narrow exceptions that may toll (pause) the statute of limitations in certain circumstances — for example, if the injured person is a minor or if the defendant left the state.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: § 9-3-90(b) — individuals under 18 when the cause of action accrues have the period run from majority (subject to § 9-3-33.1); § 9-3-94 — 'if a defendant removes from this state, the time of his absence from the state ... shall not be counted'. South Carolina: § 15-3-40 — for a person under 18 or insane when the action accrues 'the time of the disability is not a part of the time limited', but the extension cannot exceed five years for any disability except infancy nor run more than one year after the disability ceases; § 15-3-30 — a defendant's absence from the state (or continuous absence of a year or more) is not counted.
verifiedClaims.note: Both examples verified in both states. Optional citations: '(O.C.G.A. §§ 9-3-90, 9-3-94; S.C. Code §§ 15-3-40, 15-3-30)'. Georgia § 9-3-94 URL: https://law.justia.com/codes/georgia/title-9/chapter-3/article-5/section-9-3-94/.

verifiedClaims.claim: In wrongful death cases, the Georgia statute of limitations is still two years from the date of death — not from the date of the denial.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Two years under § 9-3-33 is correct for wrongful death in Georgia; South Carolina states the date-of-death accrual in the statute itself — three years for an action 'for death by wrongful act, the period to begin to run upon the death of the person' (§ 15-3-530(6)).
verifiedClaims.note: The Georgia accrual-at-death rule is settled but was not independently verified from a Georgia opinion this run; the two-year period is. Optional parity sentence for South Carolina using § 15-3-530(6).

verifiedClaims.claim: In Georgia, if the insurer can establish that you were 50% or more at fault under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, you recover nothing. In South Carolina, the threshold is 51%.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 51-12-33(g); Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co. (plaintiff recovers if his negligence is not greater than the defendant's).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33; Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243 (1991)
verifiedClaims.note: Minor precision: a jury, not the insurer, 'establishes' fault — 'if a jury finds you were 50% or more at fault' is the accurate frame.

verifiedClaims.claim: A denied injury claim is not the end. How to read the denial letter, what to gather, and the appeal and bad faith routes available.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: A denied injury claim is not the end. How to read the denial letter, what to gather, how to press for reconsideration, and when a regulatory complaint or a lawsuit is the next step.
verifiedClaims.note: Published as the Article description by roden_schema_article(). 'Appeal' and 'bad faith routes' both carry the post's core error into the structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: A denied claim is not the end. Steps include reviewing the denial letter, gathering evidence, filing appeals, bad faith complaints, or lawsuits. Georgia's bad faith statute (O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6) imposes penalties up to 50% plus attorney fees with a 60-day demand letter requirement. South Carolina's Act (S.C. Code § 38-59-20) requires no pre-suit demand. Georgia's 2-year SOL and South Carolina's 3-year SOL are not extended by a denial.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: A denied claim is not the end. Steps include reviewing the denial letter, gathering evidence, asking for reconsideration in writing, complaining to the state insurance regulator, and filing suit before the deadline. Bad-faith remedies run against your own insurer, not the other driver's: Georgia's O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6 gives a policyholder up to 50% of the loss or $5,000, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees after a 60-day demand; South Carolina awards attorney's fees after a 90-day demand (S.C. Code § 38-59-40) and recognises a bad-faith tort (Nichols v. State Farm). Georgia's 2-year and South Carolina's 3-year filing deadlines are not extended by a denial.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6; S.C. Code §§ 38-59-20, 38-59-40; Nichols v. State Farm
verifiedClaims.note: Renders in the summary box above the article. Three errors in one paragraph: § 33-4-6 framed as the reader's remedy and missing the $5,000 floor; § 38-59-20 called an 'Act' with a demand rule it does not have (it is a regulatory list; the demand statute is § 38-59-40, 90 days); 'filing appeals' as a legal step. The SOL sentence is correct.

verifiedClaims.claim: Common reasons include disputed liability, pre-existing conditions, treatment gaps, missed deadlines, policy exclusions, and insufficient evidence. The denial letter should state the reason.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34(10) (written denial; explanation on the insured's written request)
verifiedClaims.note: Publishes as FAQPage structured data. Stated as practice, not law. 'Should state the reason' is right; optional addition: 'if it does not, ask for the reasons in writing'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes. Most insurers have an internal appeals process. Your attorney can submit additional evidence and challenge the reasoning. If the appeal fails, you can file a complaint with the state insurance commissioner or sue.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: You can ask the insurer to reconsider — there is no formal appeal of a liability insurer's denial in Georgia or South Carolina, but a written request with new evidence that answers each stated reason often changes the outcome. If it does not, you can complain to the state insurance regulator (the Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire in Georgia; the Department of Insurance in South Carolina) and, before the deadline runs, file suit against the at-fault party.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34; S.C. Code § 38-59-20; oci.georgia.gov
verifiedClaims.note: Publishes as FAQPage structured data. 'Most insurers have an internal appeals process' is unverifiable and misdescribes third-party liability claims; the question itself ('Can I appeal a denied claim?') can stay because the answer reframes it.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6, unreasonable denial allows recovery of the claim plus up to 50% in penalties and attorney fees. Georgia requires a 60-day demand letter before filing.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia's bad-faith statute protects policyholders against their own insurer. Under O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6, if your insurer refuses in bad faith to pay a covered claim within 60 days of your written demand, it owes the claim plus a penalty of up to 50% of the loss or $5,000, whichever is greater, and your attorney's fees (on uninsured-motorist claims, up to 25% or $25,000 under § 33-7-11(j)). It does not let you sue the other driver's insurer for denying your claim.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6; O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11(j); Mills v. Allstate Ins. Co. (Ga. Ct. App. 2007)
verifiedClaims.note: Publishes as FAQPage structured data — the misattributed remedy is published twice over. 'Unreasonable denial' is also the wrong standard; Georgia's is a 'frivolous and unfounded refusal to pay' (Taylor v. GEICO, 2019).

verifiedClaims.claim: S.C. Code § 38-59-20 prohibits unreasonable denial, delay, or undervaluation. Remedies include claim value, consequential damages, and potentially punitive damages. No pre-suit demand is required.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina's improper-claim-practices statute, S.C. Code § 38-59-20, is enforced by the Department of Insurance and gives no private claim. A policyholder whose own insurer refuses to pay for 90 days after a demand, without reasonable cause or in bad faith, recovers attorney's fees under § 38-59-40, and under Nichols v. State Farm can sue for the bad-faith denial itself — consequential damages and, for wilful or reckless conduct, punitive damages capped by § 15-32-530. South Carolina does not allow a bad-faith suit against the other driver's insurer.
verifiedClaims.note: Publishes as FAQPage structured data. Attributes to § 38-59-20 remedies it does not provide and misses the § 38-59-40 demand period; same class of error corrected in packs 1722 and 1724.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia: 2 years from date of injury (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). South Carolina: 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). The denial does not restart or extend these deadlines.
verifiedClaims.note: Publishes as FAQPage structured data. Verified; matches the writer-profile table.

verifiedClaims.claim: Absolutely. A denied claim is not the end. An attorney can identify the issue, gather evidence, file appeals, pursue bad faith claims, and take the case to trial. We handle denied claims on contingency — you pay nothing unless we recover.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Absolutely. A denied claim is not the end. An attorney can identify the issue, gather evidence, press the insurer to reconsider, bring a bad-faith claim against your own insurer where the facts support one, and take the case against the at-fault party to trial. We handle denied claims on contingency — you pay nothing unless we recover.
verifiedClaims.note: Publishes as FAQPage structured data. 'File appeals' and 'pursue bad faith claims' carry the two core errors; the contingency sentence is the firm's own policy.

recommendedEdits: Intro: cut 'claim denials are far more common than most people expect' and the 'deny legitimate personal injury claims every day' sentence; keep the paragraph's point without a frequency claim.

Intro: rewrite the Cornell sentence — the linked Wex entry is a one-paragraph definition of 'bad faith' from the Legal Information Institute at Cornell Law School and says nothing about insurance or third-party remedies; use it only as a definition and drop 'policyholders and third-party claimants have legal remedies'.
Common reasons: soften 'One of the most overused denial tactics' to 'A common denial ground'.

Step 1: replace 'are required to provide a written explanation when they deny a claim' with the Georgia rule as it is — written denial, with an explanation on the policyholder's written request (O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34(10)) — and say no statute gives a claimant against another driver's insurer that right in either state, so ask in writing anyway; change the checklist bullet 'Deadlines for filing an appeal' to 'Any deadline the letter sets for a response'.

Step 3: rename the heading (and TOC entry) to 'Step 3 — Ask for Reconsideration in Writing'; delete 'Most insurance policies include an internal appeals process' and 'forces the insurer to re-examine your claim'; explain that there is no formal appeal of a liability insurer's denial and the letter's force is its evidence and the lawsuit it precedes; keep the checklist as a reconsideration-letter checklist; tie the 30-day deadline to O.C.G.A. § 9-11-67.1 for Georgia motor-vehicle offers; cut the 'represented claimants are far more likely' sentence.

Step 4: correct the agency name to 'Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire' (link https://oci.georgia.gov/file-consumer-insurance-complaint) and link the South Carolina Department of Insurance complaint page (https://doi.sc.gov/complaint); replace 'compel the insurer to re-open' with what the agencies do (require a written response and a thorough investigation, take enforcement action — fines and cease-and-desist orders under S.C. Code § 38-59-30 — but not value or order payment of the claim); cite O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34 and S.C. Code § 38-59-20 as claims-handling laws; reword the 'pattern' paragraph so the regulatory record is not presented as support for the claimant's own bad-faith claim.

Step 5: change 'and in some cases, directly against the insurer for bad faith conduct' to a sentence that limits bad-faith suits to the reader's own insurer and states that neither state allows one against the other driver's insurer (Mills v. Allstate; Kleckley); replace 'the vast majority ... settle' with the BJS figure (about 4% of tort cases in state courts end in a trial); remove the promise of the insurer's claim file and adjuster depositions; cut 'Lawsuits are especially common in medical malpractice cases and premises liability claims' while keeping the two internal links.

Georgia bad-faith section: open with whose remedy § 33-4-6 is (the policyholder's, against their own insurer); add '$5,000, whichever is greater'; change 'the claimant must send a written demand' to 'the policyholder'; add § 33-7-11(j) for UM claims (60-day demand; up to 25% or $25,000); replace 'no reasonable basis ... adequate investigation' with the Georgia standard — a frivolous and unfounded refusal to pay (Taylor v. GEICO, 350 Ga. App. 734 (2019)) — noting that an inadequate investigation is a regulatory practice under § 33-6-34(6); delete 'Georgia judges do enforce it'.

Nimmo); add one South Carolina sentence: a denied claim is decided at a Workers' Compensation Commission hearing on the employee's request (S.C. Comparison table: split 'Bad Faith Statute' into 'Bad-faith remedy against your own insurer' (O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6, § 33-7-11(j) | S.C. Code § 38-59-40 and Nichols v. State Farm) and 'Claims-handling law (regulator-enforced)' (O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34 | S.C. Concrete Supply Co.)' to the South Carolina comparative-fault cell and '(S.C. Code § 15-32-530, inflation-adjusted; $739,245 for 2026)' to the punitive cell.

Statute of limitations section: delete 'This is one of the shorter deadlines in the Southeast, and'; optional citations for the tolling examples (O.C.G.A. §§ 9-3-90, 9-3-94; S.C. Code §§ 15-3-40, 15-3-30) and for South Carolina wrongful death accruing at death (§ 15-3-530(6)); change 'if the insurer can establish that you were 50% or more at fault' to 'if a jury finds you were 50% or more at fault'.
Contact: change href tel:18447378587 to tel:+18447378587.

Key takeaways: rewrite per the verified text — reconsideration instead of appeals; § 33-4-6 as the policyholder's remedy with the $5,000 floor and 60-day demand; South Carolina's demand rule is § 38-59-40 (90 days) and § 38-59-20 is regulatory; keep the SOL sentence.
FAQ 2 ('Can I appeal'): replace 'Most insurers have an internal appeals process' with the reconsideration framing and name both regulators.

FAQ 3 (Georgia bad faith): restate as the policyholder's remedy against their own insurer — greater of 50% or $5,000 plus fees after a 60-day demand; § 33-7-11(j) for UM — and say it does not reach the other driver's insurer.
